title: Per-tenant dynamic burst shaping and exposure accountability for Dedicated capacity
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background:
Redwood Dedicated customers reserve throughput (RPS/Tokens) and are allowed short bursts above reservation. Current implementation uses a coarse global burst pool and a simple per-tenant leaky bucket. We've seen two classes of problems in production: 1) noisy tenants consuming disproportionate burst capacity during short spikes causing other tenants to see degraded latency; 2) billing ambiguity for partial pool degradation or temporary overcommit, leading to dispute tickets and manual SLA credit calculations.

Problem statement:
We need a per-tenant burst shaping layer that: (a) enforces fair short-term headroom allocation without causing long-tail latency, (b) produces deterministic, auditable exposure accounting for post-facto SLA credits, (c) integrates with billing ledger and rate-limiter for deterministic throttling decisions, and (d) is compatible with existing dedicated pool autoscaling and fallback policies.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Prevent single-tenant bursts from starving peers while preserving useful burst capacity for legitimate needs.
- Emit an exposure ledger per-tenant per-minute that drives SLA credit automation and customer-facing reports.
- Keep throttling decisions within 1ms of current path (no measurable p99 latency regression).
- Provide a safe migration path and retrospective backfill for 30 days to compute credits for past incidents.

Proposed design overview:
1) Burst shaping algorithm: layered token buckets. Each tenant has: (i) a reserved bucket (capacity = reservationRate * window), (ii) a rolling headroom band that grants short-term burst tokens proportional to recent steady-state usage and configured headroom share, and (iii) an emergency-burst guard tied to pool-level free capacity. Allocation policy: headroom is allocated by a weight = min(tenant_share, recent_usage_ratio) to preserve fairness when multiple tenants spike. The algorithm decays headroom smoothly over 60s to avoid oscillations.

2) Exposure accounting (immutable minute-level ledger): for every minute and tenant we record: reserved_consumed, headroom_consumed, emergency_consumed, throttled_seconds, pool_free_pressure. Ledger rows are append-only, event-sourced, and signed by the ingestion service to prevent tampering. This ledger drives automated SLA credit rules (see Acceptance Criteria) and is surfaced to customers via Console.

3) Billing integration: headroom_consumed is billed at burst-rate pricing tier. Emergency_consumed is flagged and billed at a premium or credited depending on pool health. The billing service will ingest the minute-level ledger via a scheduled consumer that validates sequence continuity and reconciles with per-token metering.

4) Throttling semantics: when headroom is exhausted, tenants are rate-limited down to reserved_rate with a soft 200ms backoff retry header for clients. Emergency bursts may be allowed for short windows when pool-level utilization < 60% but will increase exposure accounting.

5) Telemetry and alerts: expose Prometheus metrics: tenant_headroom_tokens, tenant_reserved_tokens, tenant_throttled_count, ledger_ingest_lag_seconds. Build Grafana dashboards for per-pool heatmaps and a monthly SLA-credit projection panel. Create alert rules for: ledger-ingest-failure (>1m), pool-overcommit (>95% sustained for 2m), and headroom-starvation (>10 tenants throttled in same pool simultaneously).

Data model changes:
- New table: dedicated_tenant_burst_ledger_minute (minute_ts, tenant_id, pool_id, reserved_consumed, headroom_consumed, emergency_consumed, throttled_seconds, pool_free_pressure, ingestion_signature). All fields are strings or numeric in DB; ingestion_signature is hex.
- Small addition to billing_ledger ingestion pipeline to join minute-level ledger with per-token invoice_line_items.

Backfill and migration:
- Start in canary pool (one small dedicated cluster) with new shaping disabled by default. When stable, enable shaping and ledger emission (read-only) for 7 days to validate counts.
- Run a backfill job to compute minute-level ledger for past 30 days from existing metrics to allow retroactive SLA crediting for recent incidents. Backfill will be run as lower-priority jobs in analytics cluster and results will be stored in a separate schema namespace for review.

API and Console changes:
- Console: new tenant billing view showing minute-level exposure histogram and projected credits.
- API: endpoint GET /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/burst-ledger?start=...&end=... (paginated). Requires RBAC view permission.

Acceptance criteria:
- Shaping algorithm prevents >50% of a pool's headroom being consumed by a single tenant in 60s window in canary runs.
- Ledger ingestion latency < 30s and sequence gaps < 0.1% after 2 weeks.
- Billing pipeline can produce draft SLA credit calculations for canary tenants.
- No increase in p99 request latency >5% vs baseline in canary.
- Rollout runbook and migration steps documented in Confluence.

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Week 1: Prototype token-bucket variant and unit tests, design review with PM and Billing (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/DEDICATED-BURST-SHAPING).
- Week 2: Implement ledger data model, local ingestion, and test harness.
- Week 3: Integrate with rate-limiter and add Prometheus metrics. Canary deploy to pool-qa.
- Week 4: Collect telemetry, iterate caps/decay, run backfill job for 30 days.
- Week 5: Billing integration work and Console UI rough cut.
- Week 6: Rollout to 10% production capacity with monitoring and automatic rollback flags.

Testing and QA:
- Unit tests for token allocation, decay, and fairness invariants.
- Property-based tests to assert that aggregate headroom consumption across tenants <= configured pool headroom + epsilon.
- Load tests in cluster-qa simulating correlated spikes (30 tenants spike together) and single-tenant noisy neighbor scenarios.
- End-to-end billing integration test with synthetic ledger records.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: complexity in allocation algorithm leading to unexpected starvation. Mitigation: conservative defaults, short canary windows, and ability to flip to global-burst fallback.
- Risk: ledger ingestion lag causes delayed credits. Mitigation: robust sequence checks, backpressure and retry with exponential backoff.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Do we bill headroom at same per-token rate across all customers, or introduce a dynamic premium for emergency_consumed? (Billing to decide).
- How aggressive should decay be? Shorter decay favors recent spikes but increases churn.
- Should emergency bursts be allowed for high-tier customers even under pressure? (policy decision tied to customer SLAs).

Docs and artifacts:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/DEDICATED-BURST-SHAPING
- Spike PR (prototype): https://github.com/redwood-inference/service/pull/8724
- Telemetry dashboard (draft): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd123/dedicated-burst-heatmap
